title: Nineveh Repents, and God Relents
summary: The word of the LORD comes to Jonah a second time, and this time he goes to Nineveh and proclaims that in forty days the city will be overturned. The people believe God, fast, and put on sackcloth; the king leaves his throne, sits in ashes, and decrees that everyone, even the animals, must fast and turn from violence. When God sees them turn from their evil ways, he relents from the disaster he had threatened.
story: Jonah has been swallowed, has prayed, and has been put back on dry land. Chapter 3 begins almost word for word like chapter 1, a deliberate restart: the same call, the same great city. The difference is that Jonah obeys. The book's first half showed pagan sailors turning to the LORD while the prophet fled; the second half shows a whole pagan city turning to God at a word from a reluctant prophet. The chapter ends with good news for Nineveh, but the reader who knows the book senses the question coming. Chapter 4 will reveal how Jonah feels about what God has done.
historical:
Nineveh was one of the great cities of Assyria, on the Tigris River. In the eighth century BC the Assyrian royal residence was usually at Calah (Nimrud), with Nineveh a major royal city; Sennacherib made Nineveh the capital around 700 BC and greatly enlarged it. The title "king of Nineveh" (verse 6) is unusual, since Assyrian rulers were called king of Assyria. Some take this as the storyteller's way of focusing on the city; others see it as a sign that the book is not interested in naming historical particulars; others suggest a local ruler or governor may be meant.

No Assyrian record describes a citywide repentance or a turn to Israel's God, and scholars disagree on how to weigh that silence. Some who read the book as history point to a period of instability in Assyria in the first half of the eighth century, including plague, revolts, and the solar eclipse of 763 BC, events that might have made a city receptive to a prophet's warning. Others note that such connections cannot be proven. The description of Nineveh as requiring three days to cross (verse 3) is also debated: it may refer to the time needed for a prophet to go through the city and its surrounding districts, or to the size of the greater administrative area, or be part of the story's deliberate exaggeration.
cultural:
Fasting and sackcloth were widespread signs of mourning and repentance in the ancient Near East. Sackcloth was coarse fabric, usually of goat hair, worn next to the skin; sitting in ashes or dust expressed humiliation and grief. The king's actions (rising from his throne, removing his robe, covering himself with sackcloth, sitting in ashes) reverse every sign of royal dignity, one by one. Including animals in public mourning may sound strange, but there is evidence from the ancient world of animals being included in mourning rites; the Greek historian Herodotus describes Persians shaving their horses in mourning. Whether or not that practice stands behind this verse, it shows how completely the city humbled itself, and it prepares for the book's last line, where God mentions Nineveh's cattle.

The king's decree includes the phrase "Who knows?" (verse 9), which also appears in Joel 2:14 and in David's prayer for his dying child (2 Samuel 12:22). It expresses hope without presumption: the Ninevites have no promise of mercy, only a warning of judgment, and they repent in the hope that God may yet turn.
literary: Jonah's message in verse 4 is only five words in Hebrew, the shortest prophetic sermon in the Bible, and it contains no call to repent and no offer of mercy. The rest of the chapter is dominated by the Ninevites' response, which the narrator describes at length, working from the people up to the king and then through his decree down to the animals. The key verb is "turn" (shuv), used for the Ninevites turning from their evil ways and for God perhaps turning from his anger (verses 8 to 10). The word "evil" (ra'ah) also plays two roles: the people turn from their evil, and God relents from the evil, or disaster, he had threatened. The verb in Jonah's message, "overturned" (haphak), is ambiguous: it can mean destroyed, as it does of Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:25), or turned around, changed. Nineveh was overturned, but not in the way Jonah expected.

outline.t: The second call, and Jonah goes to Nineveh
Forty days, and Nineveh will be overturned
The people believe God and fast
The king in ashes and his decree: who knows?
God sees their turning and relents

doctrines.note: The Ninevites' repentance is shown in action: they fast, humble themselves, and "turn from his evil ways and from the violence in his hands" (verse 8). God responds to what they do, not only to what they feel. Repentance means a changed direction of life.

God relents when a people turns, which shows that his warnings of judgment serve his mercy. Jeremiah 18:7-8 states the principle: if a nation God has threatened turns from its evil, he will relent. God's character, not a fixed mechanism, governs how he responds.
A foreign and hostile city believes God at a prophet's word. The book shows God's concern for the nations and anticipates the day when Gentiles would respond to the gospel.

words.note: Haphak, to overturn. The word Jonah uses for Nineveh's fate. It is the verb used for the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah, so it sounds like total destruction. But the same verb can mean to turn or be changed (for example, a heart turned in Exodus 14:5). Nineveh was indeed overturned: its people turned from their ways.

Shuv, to turn or return, here in the sense of repent. It is the Old Testament's main word for repentance, a change of direction. Used four times here, both for the Ninevites turning from evil and for the hope that God will turn from anger.

Nacham, to relent. God relented from the disaster he had threatened (verse 10). The same word describes God's response to Moses' prayer (Exodus 32:14) and to Amos's intercession (Amos 7:3, 6). It is the word Jonah will throw back at God in 4:2.

christ: Jesus drew directly on this chapter. He said, "The men of Nineveh will stand at the judgment with this generation and condemn it; for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and now One greater than Jonah is here" (Matthew 12:41). The point is sharp: pagans who heard a reluctant prophet's five-word warning repented, while Jesus' own hearers, who had heard the Son of God himself, did not. The Ninevites' repentance also anticipates the gospel going to the nations, when Gentiles who had no claim on Israel's covenants would believe and be received (Acts 11:18). And the mercy God shows here is the same mercy fully revealed in Jesus, who came not to condemn the world but to save it (John 3:17).

hard.q: Was Jonah's prophecy false, since Nineveh was not destroyed in forty days?
hard.a: Jonah announced an unconditional-sounding judgment that did not happen. Most interpreters answer that prophecies of judgment in Scripture often carry an unstated condition. Jeremiah 18:7-10 explains that if a nation God has warned turns from its evil, he will relent. The Ninevites themselves seem to have understood this, hoping that God might turn. On this view the prophecy did exactly what it was meant to do: it brought repentance, and God's relenting fulfilled his purpose. Some also note that Nineveh was eventually destroyed, in 612 BC, as Nahum announced, after its later violence. The chapter's concern is not whether Jonah's reputation as a prophet survives but whether God's mercy is right, the question Jonah himself raises in the next chapter.

questions: The Ninevites repented with no promise that God would spare them, only "Who knows?" What does their humility teach about approaching God?
The king's decree names violence as the sin to turn from. What would specific, practical repentance look like in your life right now?
Jesus said the Ninevites would condemn his generation. Why is it sometimes harder for religious insiders to repent than for outsiders?
